How Computers Execute Programs

Stage 1 Concept ⏱ 14 min 📖 Glossary

Your code never runs directly. It is fetched, decoded, and executed — billions of tiny steps per second — with memory as the workbench. Understand this and half of all future errors make sense.

🔎 Motivating questionIf a chef can hold only one recipe card at a time, how does the kitchen still produce a feast?

Objectives

  • Trace fetch-decode-execute
  • Explain CPU, memory roles
  • Describe machine code simply

Needs first: What Is Source Code?

1 Start with an analogy

Real life first, code second.

Kitchen: recipe shelf (disk storage), counter (RAM memory), chef hands (CPU). Ingredients travel shelf → counter → hands, one card at a time, blindingly fast.

⚠️ Where the analogy breaksWhere it breaks: chefs improvise, multitask, and remember. A CPU core does exactly one tiny operation per tick with zero memory of intent — all the speed comes from billions of ticks per second, not cleverness.

2 The concept, plainly

One idea at a time, words before jargon.

The CPU repeats one cycle: fetch the next instruction, decode what it means, execute it. A 3 GHz CPU does this roughly 3 billion times per second.

RAM (memory) holds the running code and its data — extremely fast, but erased when power goes. Disk/SSD keeps files for years but is far slower. Running = copy from disk to RAM, then the CPU works from RAM.

Machine code — pure numbers — is all the CPU truly understands. Java compiles to an intermediate bytecode, and the JVM converts that into machine steps on the fly.

This is why a “stuck” program still burns CPU (it is executing — just the wrong steps) and why unsaved work vanishes in a blackout (it lived only in RAM).

⚙️ Tech details — precise facts
  • Fetch–decode–execute is called the instruction cycle; each round handles one machine instruction, not one line of Java.
  • RAM is volatile (loses everything without power); SSD/disk is persistent. Save = copy RAM content to disk.
  • A program’s bytecode is platform-independent; the JVM is platform-specific — that split is what makes “write once, run anywhere” possible.

3 Watch it move: Fetch-decode-execute

Step at your pace. Text explains every move.

4 Live code demo

Small, correct Java 17 (LTS) code. Read, trace, copy.

Main.javaJava 17
public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    int a = 4;              // LOAD 4 into memory slot a
    int b = 5;              // LOAD 5 into memory slot b
    int c = a + b;          // ADD the slots into c
    System.out.println(c);  // PRINT c  -> shows 9
  }
}
▶ Output 9
  • Fetch: the CPU grabs the next instruction from RAM.
  • Decode: it figures out LOAD vs ADD vs PRINT.
  • Execute: it does it, then moves to the next line.
▶️ Run it yourselfSave exactly as Main.java, then javac Main.java and java Main. Every full program in this course works this way.
💡 Why this output?Four trivial machine steps — load, load, add, print — combine into “add and print”. Enormous speed × extreme simplicity = all computing.

6 Common mistakes (at least 3)

Wrong, why, fixed — learn from realistic slips.

❌ Mistake 1: “RAM and disk are the same thing.”Why: RAM is the counter (fast, temporary); disk is the shelf (slow, permanent). Confusing them makes “where did my file go” mysteries.
✅ Fix: Running data lives in RAM; saved files live on disk.
❌ Mistake 2: “The CPU understands Java.”Why: It understands machine numbers only. Java reaches it through two translations.
✅ Fix: Java source → bytecode → machine steps, via the JVM.
❌ Mistake 3: “Shorter code always runs faster.”Why: One short line can hide a million machine steps (a loop); ten long lines can be ten steps.
✅ Fix: Count what the machine DOES, not lines you see.

7 Guided practice

Hints first, solutions only after a real try.

Order the cycle

Put in order: A) execute B) fetch C) decode.

HintYou must collect it before you can read it.
SolutionB fetch → C decode → A execute.
RAM vs disk

A running variable lives where? The Hello.java file lives where? What survives a blackout?

HintCounter vs shelf.
SolutionVariable in RAM; Hello.java on disk; only the disk copy survives.

8 Lesson quiz

3+ questions. Attempts saved locally; review queue learns your weak spots.

9 Takeaways + next step

  • CPU: fetch → decode → execute, billions per second.
  • RAM = fast temporary counter; disk = long-term shelf.
  • Java runs via bytecode + JVM, never directly on CPU.
  • Frozen + fan = still executing (wrong steps).
🧠 Recall challengeName the three CPU steps and what each does.
